summary: Describes a mechanism for reducing the harm to MPLS traffic when a label switching router restarts its control plane, specifically its LDP component, on routers that can keep forwarding state through the restart. It is applicable to all routers.

eli5.summary: If a router's brain reboots, its hands can keep moving traffic along. This lets neighbors wait patiently and keep forwarding instead of treating it as a failure.

questions: what is the ft session tlv
how do mpls routers keep forwarding during restart
subtitle: How MPLS routers keep forwarding traffic while the LDP part of a neighbor's control plane restarts.

tldr.problem: When the LDP software on a label switching router restarts, its neighbors normally treat the label paths through it as broken, even if the router could have kept forwarding packets.
tldr.mechanism: Routers advertise an FT Session TLV in the LDP Initialization message with a Reconnect Timeout and a Recovery Time. Neighbors keep label bindings marked stale, and the restarting router refreshes its preserved forwarding entries as bindings are re-learned.
tldr.outcome: Traffic on the existing label switched paths is not disturbed, as long as the restarting router preserved its MPLS forwarding state.

facts.label: Signaled in
facts.value: FT Session TLV in the LDP Initialization message

today: RFC 3478 is a Proposed Standard from February 2003, and its metadata lists no obsoleting or updating RFC.

sections.title: Why Graceful Restart
sections.content:
When a Label Switching Router (LSR) restarts its control plane, specifically its Label Distribution Protocol (LDP) component, but can preserve its MPLS forwarding state, it is desirable not to disturb the label switched paths (LSPs) that go through it. This RFC calls the mechanism LDP Graceful Restart.

The design assumes very little. Only the actual MPLS forwarding state has to survive the restart: either incoming label -> (outgoing label, next hop) or, at an ingress, FEC -> (outgoing label, next hop). No LDP state has to be preserved.

The mechanism applies to all LSRs. Those that cannot preserve forwarding state need to implement only a subset, which does not help them, but does reduce the impact if their neighbors can preserve state. It covers downstream unsolicited label distribution; downstream on demand is left for further study.
sections.eli5: If a train station's ticket computer reboots, the trains can still run on the tracks. The idea is to keep the trains going instead of cancelling everything.

sections.title: The FT Session TLV
sections.content:
An LSR says it supports graceful restart by putting the Fault Tolerant (FT) Session TLV, defined in RFC 3479, as an optional parameter in the LDP Initialization message. The L (Learn from Network) flag MUST be 1. The other FT flags are set to 0 by the sender and ignored by the receiver.

  • FT Reconnect Timeout: milliseconds the sender would like the receiver to wait after detecting that LDP communication failed. While waiting, the receiver SHOULD keep the forwarding state for LSPs over the link between them. A value of 0 means the sender will not preserve forwarding state, but still supports the neighbor-side procedures.
  • Recovery Time: for a restarting LSR, the milliseconds it is willing to keep its preserved forwarding state, counted from when it sends the Initialization message after restart. A value of 0 means the state was not preserved or is no longer available.

The Recovery Time SHOULD be long enough for neighbors to re-sync all LSPs gracefully without congesting the LDP control plane.
sections.eli5: Each router tells its neighbors two numbers: how long to wait for me if I disappear, and how long I will hold my place after I come back.

sections.title: What the Restarting Router Does
sections.content:
After restarting its control plane, the LSR MUST check whether it preserved its MPLS forwarding state. If not, it sends Recovery Time 0. If so, it starts the MPLS Forwarding State Holding timer (its value SHOULD be configurable), marks every forwarding entry as stale, and advertises the current timer value as its Recovery Time. When the timer expires, entries still stale SHOULD be deleted. The LSR is 'restarting' while the timer runs.

While restarting, a non-egress LSR that receives a Label Mapping message looks for a forwarding entry whose outgoing label matches the label in the message and whose next hop is one of the addresses the peer sent. If found, the entry is no longer stale, the LSR ties its incoming label to the FEC in the message, and advertises that to its neighbors. For an Implicit NULL label it looks for a 'label pop' entry. If nothing matches, normal LDP procedures apply.

An egress LSR does a similar match against the next hop for the FEC, if it is configured to use the same non-NULL label for FECs sharing a next hop. If it uses a unique label per FEC, it must also preserve the FEC with each entry. If it is configured to use a NULL label, it just advertises it.
sections.eli5: After the reboot the router marks all its old notes as 'maybe out of date.' As neighbors confirm each note, it crosses off the 'maybe' and keeps using it. Notes nobody confirms are thrown away when time runs out.

sections.title: The Alternative Procedure
sections.content:
Section 3.2 describes another way for the restarting LSR. It assumes the LSR has at least as many unallocated labels as allocated ones, the allocated ones being the forwarding state it preserved.

The same holding timer, stale marking and Recovery Time apply. The difference is that while restarting, the LSR creates local label bindings using normal LDP procedures. For a given FEC it may briefly hold two bindings, the retained one and a new one, with the same outgoing label and next hop. Once the restart completes, the old one is deleted.
sections.eli5: Instead of matching each old note to a new one, the router just writes fresh notes and throws away the old ones when the timer ends.

sections.title: What Neighbors Do
sections.content:
When an LSR sees its LDP session with a neighbor go down, and the neighbor advertised the FT Session TLV, the LSR keeps the label-FEC bindings it received from that neighbor but marks them stale, and tries to re-establish the session in the usual way.

It keeps them for the lesser of the neighbor's FT Reconnect Timeout and a local, configurable Neighbor Liveness Timer. If the session does not come back in time, the stale bindings SHOULD be deleted. If it comes back and the neighbor did not preserve state, the stale bindings SHOULD be deleted at once. If the neighbor did preserve state (non-zero Recovery Time), they are kept for the lesser of the Recovery Time and a local configurable Maximum Recovery Time. The LSR SHOULD try to finish exchanging label mappings within half of the Recovery Time.

Incoming Label Mapping messages are handled normally, with three twists: stale entries are treated as if received on the new session; an identical stale binding stops being stale; and a stale binding for the same FEC with a different label is simply updated.
sections.eli5: The neighbors keep their old notes about the router but mark them 'maybe stale.' If the router comes back in time, they check the notes. If not, they throw them away.

sections.title: Label Reuse Rules
sections.content:
Once an LSR creates a label, FEC binding, it SHOULD keep the label value as long as it has a route to the FEC. If the route disappears and returns, a new binding may use a different label.

To limit mis-routing when a new binding is made, the LSR SHOULD pick the least recently used label. After releasing a label, the LSR SHOULD NOT reuse it in a binding advertised to a neighbor that supports graceful restart for at least the sum of that neighbor's FT Reconnect Timeout and Recovery Time.
sections.eli5: Do not hand out a locker number again right away, because someone might still be using the old key.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of the original LDP specification, RFC 3036, still apply. This mechanism adds denial-of-service risks. An intruder who impersonates an LDP peer can force a failure and reconnection of the TCP connection and then set the Recovery Time to 0, which forces all labels from that peer to be released. An intruder who intercepts traffic between peers could also override the Recovery Time with 0. The RFC says these attacks can be countered with an authentication scheme between LDP peers, such as the MD5-based scheme outlined in RFC 3036.

A second concern is using a label after the session that created it has expired, which could send data to the wrong destination. Because this mechanism lengthens the validity of a session by the Reconnect Timeout, the RFC requires that labels not be reused until at least the Reconnect Timeout plus Recovery Time have passed.
sections.eli5: A bad actor could pretend to be a neighbor and say 'I lost everything,' making others throw away good notes. Passwords between neighbors help prevent this.
